text.p: ** BIRTHDAYS **
American lawyer and novelist ERLE STANLEY GARDNER, who created the character 'Perry Mason', was born in 1889.
American actor JAMES CAGNEY, who began as a song-and-dance man but went on to play tough-guy roles, was born in 1899.
Australian novelist CHRISTINA STEAD was born in 1902.
Australian cyclist EDGAR 'DUNC' GRAY, who won gold at the 1932 Los Angeles Olympics, was born in 1907.
British fashion designer HARDY AMIES was born in 1909.
The Australian private secretary to Queen Elizabeth II, WILLIAM HESELTINE, was born in 1930.
British ballet dancer WAYNE SLEEP was born in 1948.

American singer, guitarist and songwriter, PHOEBE SNOW (LAUB), was born in 1952. She started her career in the early seventies and had a hit with PAUL SIMON in 1975 with "Gone at Last". After a break from the industry in the early eighties she returned with "Something Real" in 1989.

British singer, MANDY SMITH, who began her career after a much-publicised teenage relationship with the oldest 'Rolling Stone' BILL WYMAN, was born in 1970. Her hits included "I Just Can't Wait" (1987) and "Boys and Girls" (1988). In 1989 she married WYMAN and together they opened a restaurant in London
called "Sticky Fingers".
** EVENTS **
1453 : The Battle of Castillon took place between France
and England. The battle, in which the English were routed, signalled the end of the Hundred Years War between the two countries.
1790 : The first sewing machine was patented by THOMAS
SAINT of London.
1793 : CHARLOTTE CORDAY, who murdered the French
revolutionary leader JEAN-PAUL MARAT, was guillotined.
1841 : The first edition of the humourous English
magazine Punch was published.
1880 : The steamer "Centurion" and the Melbourne-bound
"Hydaspes" collided. There were no casualities.
1903 : A Royal Commission detailed the possible sites for

the new National capital. They were Tumut, Albury, Lyndhurst, Bathurst, Lake George, Orange, Armidale and Bombala. Some members of parliament wanted the constitution changed to enable the federal capital to be Melbourne or Sydney. They claimed that a capital in the form of a "mushroom town in the bush" would be "cut off from contact with the mass of citizens" and would "tend to become corrupt and sink into degeneracy". Unfortunately, they
were not listened to.
1911 : The New South Wales cabinet decided in favour of
linking the north and south of Sydney Harbour with a bridge.
1917 : The British Royal Family changed its name from the
House of Saxe-Coburg-Gotha to Windsor amid anti-German feelings in Britain during World War One.
1925 : The Australian House of Representatives passed a
bill allowing for the deportation of those not born in Australia who committed offences against industrial laws. The changes were said to be aimed at British-born Communists in the union movement.
1939 : The Federal government began issuing forms for a
National register which would enable the compilation of a list of all males between the ages of 18 and 65.
1943 : United States and Japanese navies clashed near
Bougainville.
1945 : The Potsdam Conference began between CHURCHILL,
STALIN and TRUMAN. CHURCHILL was replaced by CLEMENT ATLEE before it ended following a change of government in Britain.
1959 : The woman considered to be one of the greatest
jazz singers of all time, BILLIE HOLIDAY, died of a heroin overdose. She was 44. "Lady Day", as she would become known, started singing in Harlem clubs at the age of 15, after several
years as a prostitute.
1961 : More than 1,000 migrants rioted at the Bonegilla

camp in northern Victoria. They were discontented because they hadn't been given work as promised, and had been in the camp for months. Police used batons to quell the riot. Unemployment had reached 112,000, up 2.6 percent in a month.
1968 : The Beatles cartoon film "Yellow Submarine"
premiered at the London Pavilion.
1969 : "Oh! Calcutta", condemned as obscene because of
its nudity and profanity, opened in New York.
1974 : An IRA bomb exploded in the Tower of London,
killing one person. The attack was one of a series of IRA bombings which preceded the British parliament passing the 'Prevention of Terrorism Act'.
1979 : The 22-year-old British runner, SEBASTIAN COE,
broke JOHN WALKER's world mile record. COE clocked 3 minutes, 48.95 seconds.
1980 : Former actor, RONALD REAGAN, was chosen as the

Republican presidential candidate in the United States. Four months later REAGAN was president of the United States, having decisively defeated JIMMY CARTER by 43.9 million votes to 35.4 million. CARTER won only six of the 50 states.
1981 : More than 100 people died when suspended walkways
in the lobby of the new Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas collapsed.
1989 : Paris celebrated the Eiffel Tower's 100th
birthday.
1994 : Reports surfaced in Britain that kidnapped
Queenslander KELLIE WILKINSON and her two English companions had been murdered by the Khmer Rouge, several weeks after they had been captured in southern Cambodia.
1994 : The Shoemaker-Levy-9 comet collided with Jupiter,
generating a spectacular light show for astronomers.
1995 : Five-times world motor racing champion JUAN MANUEL
FANGIO of Argentina died.
1996 : PAUL TOUVIER, the only Frenchman to be jailed for
World War Two crimes against humanity, died. TOUVIER committed his crimes as intelligence chief of the pro-Nazi militia in the Lyon region during the final year of the German occupation.
1996 : TWA flight 800 exploded in a fireball over the
Atlantic Ocean after taking off from Kennedy Airport, New York, en route for Paris. All 230 on board died. Cause of the explosion is still unknown.
